lead: The square law assumes long channels, constant mobility and weak fields. Real transistors break all three. The vertical gate field drags carriers against the rough oxide interface, so mobility falls as the gate voltage rises: mobility degradation. The lateral drain field cannot speed carriers up beyond about 10⁷ cm/s: velocity saturation. And past pinch-off the channel gets shorter as V<sub>DS</sub> rises: channel length modulation. Together they explain why short transistors give less current than the square law predicts and why their output curves slope upward.
prereq: You need: the square-law equations from MOSFET I-V characteristics and device equations.

blocks.text: A higher V<sub>GS</sub> adds channel charge, but it also presses the electrons harder against the silicon-oxide interface, where they scatter more often. Each carrier then moves more slowly. A common fit is:
µeff = µ0 / (1 + θ·Vov), so ID = ½kn′(W/L)Vov² / (1 + θ·Vov) in saturation

µ<sub>0</sub> is the low-field mobility, k<sub>n</sub>′ = µ<sub>0</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>, and θ (in V⁻¹) is a fitted process constant, larger for thinner oxides. Doubling the overdrive now gives less than four times the current, and the transfer curve bends over. Mobility also falls as temperature rises (more lattice vibration), so the on-current of a hot chip is lower.

At low field the drift velocity is µE. At high field the carriers lose their extra energy to the lattice and the velocity levels off at v<sub>sat</sub> ≈ 10⁷ cm/s for electrons in silicon (somewhat lower for holes). A simple fit is:
v = µE / (1 + E/Ec), with critical field Ec = vsat/µ

The channel field is roughly V<sub>DS</sub>/L, so the shorter the channel, the sooner the carriers saturate. Putting this velocity into the drift integral divides the linear-region current by (1 + V<sub>DS</sub>/(E<sub>c</sub>L)). The current stops rising, and the device saturates, at

Check the limits. For a long channel (EcL ≫ Vov), VDSsat → Vov and IDsat → ½kn′(W/L)Vov², the square law. For a very short channel (EcL ≪ Vov), VDSsat is small and IDsat → W·Cox·vsat·Vov: the current is linear in overdrive and no longer depends on L. Many books fit measured devices with the alpha-power law ID ∝ Vovα, with α between 1 (fully velocity-saturated) and 2 (square law). Textbooks differ in how they define Ec (some use 2vsat/µ), so always state the model you use.

sections.h3: Channel length modulation: the moving pinch-off point

blocks.text: Past pinch-off, the extra voltage V<sub>DS</sub> − V<sub>DSsat</sub> drops across a depleted gap at the drain. As V<sub>DS</sub> rises the gap widens by ΔL and the conducting channel shortens to L − ΔL. A shorter channel carries more current, so the saturated current creeps up:

λ (V⁻¹) is a fitting parameter that grows roughly as 1/L; r<sub>o</sub> is the small-signal output resistance, the inverse of the slope of the output curve. A larger λ lowers r<sub>o</sub> and the intrinsic gain g<sub>m</sub>·r<sub>o</sub>, which is why short-channel amplifiers are harder to design. The factor applies only in saturation; in the linear region there is no pinch-off point to move.

examples.question: An nMOS has W = 1 µm, L = 0.25 µm, C<sub>ox</sub> = 8.6 fF/µm², µ<sub>n</sub> = 500 cm²/V·s, v<sub>sat</sub> = 10⁷ cm/s and λ = 0.1 V⁻¹, biased at V<sub>ov</sub> = 2 V. Find (a) the square-law saturation current, (b) E<sub>c</sub>, E<sub>c</sub>L and V<sub>DSsat</sub>, (c) the velocity-saturated current and the ratio of the two, (d) r<sub>o</sub> at that current.
steps: SI units: µ<sub>n</sub> = 0.05 m²/V·s, C<sub>ox</sub> = 8.6 × 10⁻³ F/m², v<sub>sat</sub> = 10⁵ m/s, W/L = 4.
V<sub>DSsat</sub> = 0.5 × [√(1 + 2 × 2/0.5) − 1] = 0.5 × (√9 − 1) = 1.0 V, half the square-law value of 2 V.
Check by the linear-region formula at V<sub>DS</sub> = 1.0 V: 1.72 × 10⁻³ × (2 × 1 − 1²/2)/(1 + 1/0.5) = 1.72 × 10⁻³ × 1.5/3 = 0.86 mA. ✓
examples.answer: Square law 3.44 mA; velocity saturation gives 0.86 mA at V<sub>DSsat</sub> = 1.0 V, four times less; r<sub>o</sub> ≈ 11.6 kΩ. (With L = 2 µm the same formula gives V<sub>DSsat</sub> = 1.66 V, close to the square-law 2 V.)

examples.question: A long-channel nMOS has k<sub>n</sub>′(W/L) = 2 mA/V² and θ = 0.25 V⁻¹. Find the saturation current at V<sub>ov</sub> = 1 V and 2 V with and without mobility degradation.
steps: Ideal: ½ × 2 × 1² = 1.0 mA and ½ × 2 × 2² = 4.0 mA.
Doubling V<sub>ov</sub> multiplies the current by 2.67/0.80 = 3.33, not 4.
examples.answer: 0.80 mA and 2.67 mA (ideal 1.0 and 4.0 mA); the degraded curve grows by 3.33 instead of 4 when the overdrive doubles.

traps: Mobility degradation comes from the vertical gate field, velocity saturation from the lateral drain field; only velocity saturation makes the current linear in V<sub>ov</sub>.
For a short channel V<sub>DSsat</sub> is less than V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>; using the square-law V<sub>DSsat</sub> puts the device in the wrong region.
Convert units first: cm²/V·s × 10⁻⁴ gives m²/V·s, fF/µm² × 10⁻³ gives F/m², cm/s × 10⁻² gives m/s.
λ is a fitted number that grows as L shrinks, not a material constant.

quiz.q: Define velocity saturation and give v<sub>sat</sub> for electrons in silicon.
quiz.a: At high lateral field the drift velocity stops rising with field and levels off, because carriers lose energy to the lattice; v<sub>sat</sub> ≈ 10⁷ cm/s.

quiz.q: Why does the saturated output curve of a real MOSFET slope upward?
quiz.a: Raising V<sub>DS</sub> widens the depleted gap at the drain and moves the pinch-off point towards the source, so the conducting channel shortens and carries more current. (1 + λV<sub>DS</sub>) models the rise.

quiz.q: µ<sub>n</sub> = 400 cm²/V·s and v<sub>sat</sub> = 10⁷ cm/s. Find E<sub>c</sub> in V/cm and V/m.
L = 0.18 µm, E<sub>c</sub> = 2 × 10⁶ V/m, V<sub>ov</sub> = 1.2 V. Find V<sub>DSsat</sub> and compare it with the square law.
quiz.a: E<sub>c</sub>L = 0.36 V. V<sub>DSsat</sub> = 0.36 × [√(1 + 2.4/0.36) − 1] = 0.36 × (2.769 − 1) = 0.637 V, about half the square-law 1.2 V.

quiz.q: A short device shows I<sub>D</sub> almost linear in V<sub>ov</sub> and g<sub>m</sub> nearly constant. Which effect dominates, and why not mobility degradation?
quiz.a: Velocity saturation: with I<sub>Dsat</sub> ≈ WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub>V<sub>ov</sub>, g<sub>m</sub> ≈ WC<sub>ox</sub>v<sub>sat</sub> is constant. Mobility degradation only bends the square law; its g<sub>m</sub> keeps rising with V<sub>ov</sub>, just more slowly.

quiz.q: Two transistors differ only in L, the second twice as long, and carry the same current. Compare λ and r<sub>o</sub>.
quiz.a: λ ∝ 1/L, so λ halves; r<sub>o</sub> = 1/(λI<sub>D</sub>) doubles. The longer device is the better current source.

beyond: Production models such as BSIM4 use many parameters for these effects and solve the lateral field inside the channel. Series source and drain resistance also flattens the curves and is easily mistaken for velocity saturation; it is covered in MOSFET capacitances and parasitic resistances. Search for "alpha-power law MOSFET" and "gm/ID design" to go further.

figure.caption: The device of the first worked example at an overdrive of 2 V. The dashed square law would reach 3.44 mA; with velocity saturation the current stops at 0.86 mA once V<sub>DS</sub> reaches 1.0 V. The dotted line is the small upward slope that channel length modulation adds in saturation.

spec.aria: Drain current against drain voltage: a dashed square-law curve rising to 3.44 milliamps at 2 volts, and a solid velocity-saturated curve flattening at 0.86 milliamp from 1.0 volt, with a dotted line of slope lambda times I D beyond it.
